clinicalPearls: A rare disorder of follicular keratinisation causing widespread spiny follicular papules with progressive scarring alopecia of the scalp, eyebrows and eyelashes
The classic X-linked form is caused by variants in MBTPS2, the same gene implicated in IFAP syndrome, giving considerable clinical overlap
Facial follicular keratoses often appear in infancy, followed by cicatricial loss of eyebrows, lashes and scalp hair
Photophobia and corneal changes can occur, echoing the ocular involvement of IFAP syndrome
Palmoplantar keratoderma and nail changes are reported in some patients
Diagnosis is clinical, supported by biopsy showing follicular hyperkeratosis and perifollicular inflammation with later scarring, and by MBTPS2 molecular testing
Management is supportive with keratolytics and emollients, treatment of secondary inflammation and infection, and ophthalmology input for ocular involvement
reference.pathophysiology: Keratosis follicularis spinulosa decalvans is usually caused by variants in MBTPS2, encoding a membrane-bound zinc metalloprotease required for regulated intramembrane proteolysis governing sterol and lipid homeostasis and the endoplasmic reticulum stress response. Disturbed function impairs follicular keratinisation, producing spiny follicular plugs, while chronic perifollicular inflammation gradually destroys hair follicles to give a scarring (cicatricial) alopecia. Because the same gene underlies IFAP syndrome, the two conditions represent an allelic spectrum with overlapping cutaneous and ocular features.
additionalInvestigations: Skin/scalp biopsy showing follicular hyperkeratosis, perifollicular inflammation and later fibrosis
Ophthalmological assessment including slit-lamp examination for corneal changes
Bacterial swabs where secondary infection is suspected
redFlags: Recurrent secondary infection of inflamed follicular lesions
Features suggesting the broader IFAP phenotype
reference.prognosis: The follicular keratoses may improve after puberty, but the associated scarring alopecia is permanent; visual prognosis depends on the extent of corneal involvement.
pitfalls: Not recognising the shared MBTPS2 basis and overlap with IFAP syndrome
Mistaking early disease for ordinary keratosis pilaris and missing the scarring alopecia
Neglecting ophthalmological surveillance for corneal disease
Delaying anti-inflammatory measures that might limit follicular scarring
